# LSASS Memory Dump With comsvcs.dll MiniDump

`win_proc_lsass_dump_comsvcs` · Sigma id `83a12117-5a73-41a1-8841-b024282e9a3e` · status `experimental` · level `high`

## Goal

Catch credentials being stolen from memory with a tool already built into Windows: rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll's MiniDump function to write a dump of LSASS, the process that holds logged-on users' password hashes and Kerberos tickets.

## ATT&CK

- [T1003.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/) LSASS Memory
- Tactic: Credential Access (TA0006)

Checked against pinned ATT&CK v20.1 by `ringtail validate`.

## Log source

product: `windows`, category: `process_creation`

## Detection logic

Fires when rundll32 (matched by path or original file name) loads comsvcs.dll and calls its MiniDump export, by name or by its ordinal number (#24, used to dodge string matching). Matching is case-insensitive, so mixed-case tricks don't help.

Exact logic, generated from the rule:

- **selection_img**: any one of
  - `Image` ends with `'\rundll32.exe'`
  - `OriginalFileName` is `'RUNDLL32.EXE'`
- **selection_dll**: `CommandLine` contains `'comsvcs'`
- **selection_export**: `CommandLine` contains any of `'MiniDump'`, `'#24'`
- **Condition**: `all of selection_*`

## SIEM queries

Generated from the rule by `ringtail convert`. Check the field names against your own
data before deploying: they assume the schema noted for each query.

**Splunk (SPL)**: Windows event and Sysmon field names (Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows / Sysmon)

```spl
(Image="*\\rundll32.exe" OR OriginalFileName="RUNDLL32.EXE") CommandLine="*comsvcs*" (CommandLine IN ("*MiniDump*", "*#24*"))
```

**Microsoft Sentinel / Defender XDR (KQL)**: Defender XDR DeviceProcessEvents (also in Sentinel with the Defender XDR connector)

```kql
DeviceProcessEvents
| where (FolderPath endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "RUNDLL32.EXE") and ProcessCommandLine contains "comsvcs" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "MiniDump" or ProcessCommandLine contains "#24")
```

## Known false positives

- Very rare. Some support or crash-diagnostic scripts dump non-LSASS processes this way; check the process ID in the command line

## Triage steps

1. Find the target process ID (the number after MiniDump) and check whether it was LSASS at that time. It almost always is. Note the dump file path.
2. Check the parent process and how it started: WmiPrvSE.exe, services.exe, or a remote service install points to remote execution from another host (lsassy and similar tools work this way). Find that source host; it's likely compromised too.
3. Look for the dump file being read or copied off (SMB access to the path, archive tools) and delete it as part of containment.
4. Treat every account logged on to that host as compromised: reset passwords, revoke sessions, and check those accounts for logons elsewhere.
5. Coverage gap: other LSASS dump methods (ProcDump, nanodump, direct API calls from malware) don't go through comsvcs.dll. Pair this rule with LSASS process-access monitoring (Sysmon event 10) or EDR credential-theft alerts.

## Test results

**PASS**: 3/3 true-positive samples matched, 3/3 false-positive samples correctly ignored.

| Sample | Should fire | Fired | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| The common form: MiniDump by name, LSASS PID, full dump to Temp. | yes | yes | pass |
| Export called by ordinal #24 to dodge the MiniDump string. | yes | yes | pass |
| Mixed case through PowerShell. | yes | yes | pass |
| Near miss: rundll32 opening a Control Panel applet. | no | no | pass |
| Near miss: comsvcs.dll loaded by rundll32 for something other than MiniDump. | no | no | pass |
| Out of scope: a sanctioned ProcDump crash dump of an app. A different tool, so this rule doesn't cover it either way. | no | no | pass |
